defaults.permitted_development: Across Warwickshire, roof-lights are often permitted development where they stay low-profile, project no more than 150mm from the roof plane and do not rise above the existing roof height. The straightforward route can disappear if the property is listed, subject to local restrictions or if the proposal starts to read as a roof enlargement rather than a simple skylight.

rules.height_rules: Across Warwickshire, height control for a roof-light is simple but strict: the proposal should not rise above the existing roof. The more flush and subordinate the unit appears, the easier the scheme is to keep within the normal householder route.
rules.depth_rules: Across Warwickshire, keep the projection tight to the existing slope. The normal roof-light limit is 150mm, and anything noticeably prouder than that risks being treated as a more substantial roof alteration.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Warwickshire, roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: Across Warwickshire, roof-lights are treated as minor roof alterations, not full roof enlargements, so the existing roof form should remain dominant. Roof terraces, raised platforms and larger roof additions sit outside the normal roof-light route.
rules.materials_rules: Across Warwickshire, choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even small roof-lights can need closer scrutiny if they are proposed on prominent slopes or on buildings with a consistent historic roofscape.
restrictions.listed_building: Roof-lights in listed buildings are commonly treated as heritage works because the roof covering, structure and external appearance all contribute to significance.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the standard roof-light allowance survives everywhere: Article 4 controls and site-specific conditions can require an application for visible roof changes.

rules.permitted_development: In Nuneaton and Bedworth, a simple skylight or roof-light is commonly permitted development provided it remains a minor roof alteration, projects no more than 150mm from the slope and does not exceed the roof's existing height. Heritage controls, local restrictions and larger roof changes can all take the work outside that simpler route.

rules.height_rules: The alteration must not exceed the height of the existing roof. In practice that means choosing a low-profile unit that sits quietly within the roof slope rather than reading as an added structure on top of it.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is controlled by projection from the roof plane rather than by the size of the opening alone. Once the unit projects more than 150mm, the straightforward householder route is usually lost.
rules.boundary_rules: Roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: Roof-lights are treated as minor roof alterations, not full roof enlargements, so the existing roof form should remain dominant. Roof terraces, raised platforms and larger roof additions sit outside the normal roof-light route.
rules.materials_rules: Use flashings, frame colours and glazing details that sit quietly within the existing roof. The closer the finish is to the host roof covering and the less bulky the frame, the easier it is to keep the alteration visually subordinate.

restrictions.conservation_area: A roof-light in a conservation area is usually easiest to justify when it is discreetly placed and does not disrupt an established roof form.
restrictions.listed_building: Installing roof-lights in a listed building, or altering historic roof fabric within its curtilage, can require listed building consent even where the unit looks modest.
restrictions.article4_notes: Roof-specific planning conditions and Article 4 directions are a common reason why an otherwise modest roof-light still needs planning permission.

rules.roof_rules: Think of a roof-light as a small insertion into the existing slope, not as a way to reshape the roof. Larger additions, terraces and platforms are outside the ordinary roof-light allowance.

rules.permitted_development: In Stratford on Avon, a modest roof-light on a house is usually permitted development if it projects no more than 150mm from the existing roof slope, does not exceed the height of the existing roof and the property still benefits from normal householder rights. Planning permission becomes more likely where the work is on a listed building, in a controlled area or tied to a wider roof enlargement.

rules.boundary_rules: If the proposal creates a side-facing window, it should be obscure-glazed and any opening part should have its lowest edge at least 1.7 metres above the floor level of the room. Privacy and visible road-facing roof slopes deserve the earliest check.
